zh: 先把每个人的三个值排序成 a ≤ b ≤ c。不同对手可以用不同的出场顺序，所以每一对选手只需判断“是否存在一种配对让 X 严格赢两局”。
X 能击败 Y 当且仅当 bX > aY 且 cX > bY：用 X 的中间值打 Y 的最小值、X 的最大值打 Y 的中间值即可赢两局；反过来，任何赢两局的方案都必须满足这两个不等式。
于是 X 需要满足：bX 大于其他所有人 a 的最大值，cX 大于其他所有人 b 的最大值。分别求 a 列、b 列的最大值、最大值所属的人、以及排除该人后的次大值（可以与最大值相等）；检查每个人时若他自己就是最大值的拥有者，就用次大值比较；严格大于才算赢，计数输出。
en: First sort each player's three values into a <= b <= c. Different opponents may be met with different orders, so for each pair of players you only need to know whether some pairing lets X win two rounds strictly.

X beats Y exactly when bX > aY and cX > bY: send X's middle value against Y's smallest and X's largest against Y's middle to win two rounds; conversely, any plan that wins two rounds forces both inequalities.

So X needs bX to exceed the largest a among all other players and cX to exceed the largest b among all other players. For columns a and b, find the maximum, the player who owns it, and the second largest after excluding that player (it may equal the maximum); when checking a player who owns the maximum, compare with the second largest instead; only strictly greater counts as a win; count and print.

explanationEn:
## Fixed source correction and this site's range

The fixed OAMaster commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc, file fastprep/Amazon/amazon-find-capable-winners.md, states clearly: X can beat Y if there exists some pairing permutation of the two sides under which X strictly wins at least two rounds; it is not required that one permutation beats all permutations of Y. The original text shows that X=[9,5,11] and Y=[7,12,3] can beat each other. The wording "any rearrangement" in the early #7 summary does not match the original "some rearrangement", and this site corrects it according to the original; the source implementations in three languages that sort and compare the majority at the same positions are also incorrect, and they are neither executed nor reused.

The original file requires each player's three values to be distinct, but the #7 summary does not restrict duplicates. This site explicitly keeps the wider input domain in which each triple may contain repeated values, still judged by the strict winning definition above; this is a range extension, not a claim that the original problem allows duplicates. Both the raw text and the summary specify 2<=n<=100000 and boost values 1..10^9, and n=1 is not added. The standard I/O was added by this site and does not change the semantics that different opponents may be met with different permutations. The same complete original problem also corresponds to the already included #142, but this ID rebinds all its sources, package, and verification evidence.

## Proof of correctness

Sort each triple as a<=b<=c. X can beat Y if and only if bX>aY and cX>bY: if two strict wins exist, arrange the two winning values of X by size; the smaller one is at most bX, while the smaller of the two defeated values is at least aY; the larger winning value is at most cX, while the larger defeated value of the opponent is at least bY, which gives the necessary condition. Conversely, pairing bX with aY and cX with bY directly wins two rounds.

Therefore each player only needs to exceed the largest minimum value and the largest middle value among all other players. For each of these two columns, record the maximum, the player who owns the maximum, and the second largest after excluding that player; the second largest may equal the maximum. When checking, exclude exactly the player themself. The player must not be included in the comparison set: for example with [2,2,2] against [1,1,1], the first player can win, but a maximum of the minimum values that includes the player themself would wrongly reject them.

Sorting three numbers is a constant-time operation, and building the extremes and checking each player are both O(n), for O(n) total time and O(n) space. Strictly greater is used; a tie is not a win. The answer can be 0 or n. The independent oracle enumerates the six relative permutations for every pair and does not use the sorted inequality above.

## Checking the examples

Under the correct rule, the original four-player example of the #7 summary gives 2, with the 2nd and 4th players as winners; the source's same-position majority code wrongly counts only the 4th player. In the raw two-player example both players can beat each other, so the answer is also 2. This site adds an example with two [1,1,1] players containing repeated values: nobody can strictly win two rounds, so the answer is 0.
